# Basics of embryology

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Basics of pediatrics > Basics of embryology*

[Original Article Link](/library/uo0pdS)

---

## Summary

Embryology is the study of the origin and prenatal development of an organism, comprising the germinal (first two weeks from <u>conception</u>), embryonic (third to eighth week from <u>conception</u>), and <u>fetal period</u> (ninth week from <u>conception</u> until <u>birth</u>). <u>Gestation</u> in embryology refers to <u>conceptional age</u>, i.e., the time period from <u>conception</u> to <u>birth</u>, and should be distinguished from <u>gestational age</u>, an obstetrics term, which is measured in weeks following the first day of the mother's <u>last menstrual period</u>. Primordial cells develop during the <u>embryonic period</u> and migrate to the developing <u>gonads</u>. Further maturation into fertile <u>oocytes</u> and spermatozoa occurs via <u>meiosis</u> during different stages of male and female organism development. <u>Embryonic stem cells</u> are <u>pluripotent</u> and can differentiate into almost any type of tissue, thus being of great interest in the research and development of new therapeutic approaches. For more information on the morphogenesis of organ systems, see the article on <u>embryogenesis</u>.

---

## Overview

* Definition: the study of the origin and prenatal development of an organism.

* Timing: The periods of <u>embryonic development</u> are measured from the actual point of <u>conception</u> (i.e. <u>conceptional age</u>).





| <br>Periods of <u>embryonic development</u> [[1]](/library/ZzbZrw) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Period | <u>Conceptional age</u> | Events |
| Germinal period | 1–2 weeks | <br><br>* <u>Fertilization</u><br><br>* <u>Implantation of the blastocyst</u> in the <u>uterus</u><br><br>* <u>Amnion</u> formation<br><br><br> |
| Embryonic period | 3–8 weeks | <br><br>* Differentiation of head, limbs, and torso<br><br>* <u>Organogenesis</u><br><br>* Highly susceptible to <u>teratogens</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Fetal period</u> | <br>9 weeks to <u>birth</u><br> | <br>* Growth and differentiation of tissue and organs formed during the <u>embryonic period</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Organ system development begins during the <u>embryonic period</u>, while organ maturation occurs during the <u>fetal period</u>!

---

## Germ cell development (gametogenesis)

### Primordial <u>germ cell development</u>




* Occurs during the 4<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>

* Primordial germ cells arise from the <u>yolk sac</u> and migrate to the developing <u>gonads</u> of the <u>urogenital folds</u>.

* After <u>meiosis</u>, primordial germ cells mature to sex-specific <u>gametes</u> (<u>oocytes</u> and spermatozoa).





### Germline




* Definition: the cells that develop into mature germ cells (gametes), which pass genetic material on to progeny

* Process: involves <u>meiosis</u> of primordial germ cells within the <u>gonads</u>

* <u>Oogenesis</u> (development and maturation of the <u>ova</u>): the production of an <u>oocyte</u> with 2–3 polar bodies

* <u>Spermatogenesis</u> (<u>sperm</u> cell development): production of four functional spermatids





> [!NOTE]
> Four functional spermatids or an <u>oocyte</u> with three <u>polar bodies</u> are produced from one primordial germ cell.




> [!NOTE]
> All of the <u>oocytes</u> that will ever be produced are formed during the <u>fetal period</u>, whereas <u>sperm</u> production begins at <u>puberty</u> and never stops!

---

## Meiosis

### Overview  [[2]](/library/UIabXN)[[3]](/library/W5YPQp)




* Definition: germ cell maturation in which four daughter cells with a recombinant <u>genome</u> are produced from one germ cell

* Process: <u>Meiosis</u> involves two major phases (referred to as <u>meiosis I</u> and <u>meiosis II</u>) occurring after <u>DNA replication</u> during the <u>S phase</u> of <u>interphase</u>.

* Meiosis I (equatorial division)

* Synapsis (syndesis): the pairing of <u>homologous chromosomes</u>

* Genetic recombination: Individual <u>chromosome</u> segments are exchanged between the maternal and paternal <u>chromatids</u> of <u>homologous chromosomes</u> (recombination) in a process known as <u>crossing over</u>.

* <u>Chromosome</u> number reduction:

* A <u>diploid</u> set of <u>chromosomes</u> is divided in half when the <u>homologous chromosomes</u> separate from one another.

* Disjunction of <u>chromosomes</u> occurs without <u>centromere</u> splitting generating 2 <u>haploid</u> daughter cells, each with 23 <u>chromosome</u> pairs.

* Meiosis II (nuclear division):

* Generally corresponds to the phases of <u>mitosis</u>

* <u>Sister chromatids</u> of each <u>chromosome</u> from the <u>haploid</u> set separate from each other.

* Disjunction occurs with <u>centromere</u> splitting; each cell entering <u>meiosis II</u> produces 2 daughter cells, each with 23 <u>chromosomes</u>.

* Result

* Cell number: 1 mother cell → 4 daughter cells

* Set of <u>chromosomes</u>: <u>diploid</u> mother cell (2n)  → <u>haploid</u> daughter cell (1n)

* <u>DNA</u> content: 4 <u>chromatids</u> of the mother cell (4C) → 1 <u>chromatid</u> per daughter cell (1C)

* For sex-specific features, see <u>female reproductive organs</u> and <u>male reproductive organs</u>.

### Stages of <u>meiosis I</u>




|  | Stage | Number of cells | <u>Chromosome</u> set | <u>DNA</u> content |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prophase I | <br><br>* Leptotene<br><br>* <u>Chromosomes</u> condense and become visible<br><br>* <u>Chromosomes</u> attach to the <u>nuclear envelope</u><br><br>* Zygotene<br><br>* Synapsis (syndesis): The pairing of <u>homologous chromosomes</u>.<br><br>* Formation of the synaptonemal complex occurs.<br><br>* Pachytene<br>* Crossing over: The <u>chromatids</u> crossover (form chiasmata) and exchange genetic material, resulting in genetic recombination of <u>homologous chromosomes</u>.<br><br>* Diplotene<br><br>* The synaptonemal complex disappears.<br><br>* <u>Homologous chromosomes</u> begin to separate, but continue to be held together by the <u>chiasmata</u> (crossover site).<br><br>* Diakinesis<br><br>* The <u>nuclear membrane</u> disintegrates.<br><br>* The <u>spindle apparatus</u> begins to form.<br><br><br> | <br>* 1<br><br> | <br>* 2n<br><br> | <br>* 4C<br><br> |
| Metaphase I | <br>* <u>Chromosome</u> pairs align at the <u>equatorial plane</u>.<br><br> |  |  |  |
| Anaphase I | <br>* <u>Homologous chromosome</u> pairs separate via the disintegration of the <u>chiasmata</u>.<br><br> |  |  |  |
| Telophase I | <br>* <u>Cell membrane</u> pinches in at the equator, causing the <u>diploid cell</u> to divide into two <u>haploid cells</u>.<br><br> | <br>* 2<br><br> | <br>* 1n<br><br> | <br>* 2C<br><br> |





### Stages of <u>meiosis II</u>




| Stage | Description | Number of cells | <u>Chromosome</u> set | <u>DNA</u> content |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prophase II | <br><br>* <u>Chromosomes</u> condense.<br><br>* Formation of the <u>spindle apparatus</u> occurs.<br><br><br> | <br>* 2<br><br> | <br>* 1n<br><br> | <br>* 2C<br><br> |
| Metaphase II | <br>* <u>Chromosomes</u> align at the <u>equatorial plane</u>.<br><br> |  |  |  |
| Anaphase II | <br><br>* The two <u>chromatids</u> of each <u>chromosome</u> separate at the <u>centromere</u>.<br><br>* <u>Chromatids</u> migrate to <u>the cell</u> poles.<br><br><br> |  |  |  |
| Telophase II | <br><br>* The <u>nuclear envelope</u> reorganizes.<br><br>* <u>Cell membrane</u> pinches in at the equator.<br><br>* <u>The cell</u> divides into two <u>haploid cells</u>, each with one single <u>chromatid</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* 4<br><br> | <br>* 1n<br><br> | <br>* 1C<br><br> |

## Stem cells

* Definition: cells capable of differentiating into specialized cells (<u>potency</u>) as well as replicating while maintaining their undifferentiated state (self-renewal)

* Cell division

* Symmetric division: Both daughter cells have <u>stem cell</u> properties.

* Asymmetric division: One daughter cell is a copy of the mother <u>stem cell</u> and the other one is a precursor cell with differentiated properties.

* Characteristics

* Totipotency (<u>omnipotency</u>): the ability of a cell to differentiate into all cell types, including extraembryonic (<u>placental</u>) cells

* Pluripotency: the ability of a cell to differentiate into all cell types, with the exception of extraembryonic cells (for example, the cells of the <u>ectoderm</u>, which can differentiate into nerve or <u>skin</u> cells, but not into other germ layer cells)

* Multipotency: the ability of a cell to differentiate into more than one related cell type (for example, <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u>, which can differentiate into myeloid or lymphoid cells)

* Classification

* Embryonic stem cells (ESCs)

* <u>Pluripotent cells</u> that can only develop into embryonic cells, but not trophoblastic cells

* Originate from the inner cell mass during the blastocyte stage

* Adult stem cells

* <u>Pluripotent cells</u> that provide a supply of cells for regenerative tissue

* Originate from differentiated tissues with high replication <u>potency</u> (e.g., <u>bone marrow</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation</u> is used to treat hemato-oncologic conditions, e.g., <u>leukemias</u>.

| <br>* Pax <u>proteins</u><br><br> | <br>* Differentiation of the <u>paraxial mesoderm</u><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* <u>Zinc finger</u> <u>proteins</u><br><br> | <br>* Activation or inhibition of <u>genes</u> for growth and differentiation<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* <u>Helix-loop-helix</u> <u>proteins</u><br><br> | <br>* Regulation of muscle development<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* <u>Testis-determining factor</u> (<u>TDF</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Development of male <u>gonads</u><br><br>* <u>Anti-Mullerian hormone</u> expression through induction of the <u>gene</u> SOX-9<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>Growth factors<br> | <br>* Transforming growth factor β (<u>TGF-β</u>) superfamily<br><br> | <br>* Development of <u>skeletal muscle</u> and the <u>extracellular matrix</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Epidermal growth factor (<u>EGF</u>) family<br><br> | <br>* Differentiation of the nervous system<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* <u>Fibroblast</u> growth factor (FGF) superfamily<br><br> | <br><br>* Produced at the apical ectodermal ridge<br><br>* Regulates development of the limbs by enhancing <u>mitosis</u> of the mesodermal cells<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* <u>Insulin-like growth factor</u> (<u>IGF</u>) family<br><br> | <br>* Skeletal and muscle growth<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Nerve growth factor (NGF) family<br><br> | <br>* Neuronal survival and differentiation<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Hedgehog (e.g., sonic hedgehog gene)<br><br> | <br><br>* Produced at the <u>notochord</u><br><br>* Is highly expressed at the zones of polarizing activity   at the base of limb buds<br><br>* Regulates differentiation of <u>somites</u> along the anteroposterior axis and the <u>neural tube</u><br><br>* Mutations cause <u>holoprosencephaly</u> (due to failed forebrain cleavage)<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Wnt (e.g., <u>Wnt-7 gene</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Produced at the apical ectodermal ridge<br><br>* Required for organization of body structures along the <u>dorsoventral axis</u><br><br>* Regulates development of <u>kidneys</u> and limbs and muscle <u>cell differentiation</u><br><br><br> |  |  |
| <u>Cell adhesion molecules</u> | <br>* <u>Immunoglobulin</u> superfamily (e.g., neural <u>cell adhesion molecule</u> )<br><br> | <br>* Binding of a <u>neuron</u> to a neighboring cell<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Cadherins</u> (<u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>-dependent <u>transmembrane proteins</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Cell-to-cell adhesion (e.g., as a component of <u>desmosomes</u>)<br><br>* Increased expression of <u>E-cadherin</u>, for example, mediates binding between blastomeres.<br><br>* Decreased expression of <u>E-cadherin</u> enables cell migration during <u>embryogenesis</u>.<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* <u>Integrins</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Binding to the <u>extracellular matrix</u><br><br>* Involved in cell migration, cell division, <u>cell differentiation</u>, etc.<br><br><br> |  |  |
| Intercellular channels | <br>* <u>Gap junctions</u> (<u>nexus</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Communication between neighboring cells<br><br>* Facilitation of signaling molecules (e.g., <u>retinoic acid</u>) channel crossing to regulate <u>gene</u> activity.<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Extracellular matrix</u> | <br><br>* <u>Collagen</u><br><br>* <u>Glycosaminoglycans</u><br><br>* <u>Proteoglycans</u><br><br>* Glycoproteins<br><br><br> | <br>* Binding, transportation, and distribution of signaling molecules<br><br> |  |
| Relevant <u>hormones</u> involved in <u>embryogenesis</u> | <br>* <u>Androgens</u> (<u>testosterone</u> )<br><br> | <br>* Differentiation of sexual organs<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Thyroxine</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Transcription</u> modulation of various <u>genes</u> through <u>intracellular receptors</u>, e.g., those for <u>CNS</u> development<br><br> |  |  |
